costGuide.title: Mercedes-Benz OM629 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an OM629 engine typically takes 15-20 hours at £75-£95/hr (independent specialist) - the engine bay is incredibly tight, often requiring a subframe drop or engine-out approach via the top.
paragraphs: What genuinely moves the price for this engine is the condition of the piezo-electric injectors and the twin turbocharger oil feed lines. Because the OM629 is a highly complex V8, recon specialists will typically strip the entire top end to clean carbon buildup, replace all turbo oil lines as standard, and verify the piezo injector spray patterns. For a full breakdown of market rates, see our full reconditioned engine cost guide.

failures.title: Mercedes-Benz OM629 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Turbocharger Oil Feed Coking - Bi-turbo setup
items.whatHappens: The twin turbochargers rely on specific oil feed lines that are prone to heat-soak and coking, especially if oil change intervals were extended or incorrect oil specs were used. Restricted oil flow starves the turbo bearings, leading to shaft play, severe whining, blue smoke, and eventual catastrophic turbo failure.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught before the turbos destroy themselves, the oil feed lines and banjo bolts can be replaced. If the turbos have failed and sent metal through the engine, a full replacement unit is required.

items.title: Injector Seal Weeping ("Black Death") - All variants
items.whatHappens: The copper washer seals at the base of the piezo-electric injectors degrade over time, allowing high-pressure combustion gases to escape. This creates a black, crusty carbon buildup around the injector heads, leading to a distinct tapping noise, rough idling, and a strong smell of exhaust in the cabin.
items.repairVsReplace: This is a routine maintenance item, not a terminal failure. Replacing the seals and cleaning the cylinder head is inexpensive and should be done preventatively.

items.title: EGR and Swirl Flap Carbon Buildup - All variants
items.whatHappens: The complex intake manifold houses swirl flaps that become clogged with EGR soot over time, restricting airflow and triggering limp mode. This is exacerbated by the V8 layout, which traps heat and accelerates carbon deposition.
items.repairVsReplace: Intake manifolds often require replacement or professional ultrasonic cleaning. A verified swirl flap delete is a common and effective preventative measure performed during a rebuild.

failures.goodYearsLine: The OM629 resolved several of the OM628's early teething issues with revised piezo injectors and better engine management, making it a more robust unit overall. However, units with meticulously documented turbo oil line maintenance are highly prized, as neglected examples can easily generate repair bills that exceed the host vehicle's entire market value .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the Mercedes-Benz OM629
variants.intro: The engine code is stamped on the left-hand side of the cylinder block, near the bellhousing. It will also be listed on your V5C logbook under "Engine Capacity" or visible via a VIN decode. The OM629 is frequently confused with its predecessor, the OM628 (which used solenoid injectors and had earlier teething issues), or the later 3.0L V6 OM642 which eventually took over the flagship diesel role. Fitting the wrong revision or assuming interchangeability matters significantly: the OM629 requires specific ECU mapping for its piezo-electric injectors, distinct turbo plumbing, and different engine mount configurations that will not function correctly if swapped with an OM628 or an OM642.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement OM629 Engine - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used OM629 engine is an extreme financial risk unless it comes with verifiable, recent documentation of a turbo oil feed line upgrade and injector seal replacement. Given the engine-out labour required to fix these items, buying a used unit with unknown history often leads to an immediate £3,000+ teardown bill.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned OM629 engine is the only sensible choice for most buyers. A reputable rebuild will proactively address the fatal flaws by installing upgraded turbo oil feed lines, verifying piezo injector spray patterns, and replacing all injector seals, while ultrasonically cleaning the complex intake manifold.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full OM629 engine rebuild is justified for pristine X164 GL-Class or W221 S-Class restorations where maximum longevity and originality are required. An upgraded rebuild should include line-boring, balanced internals, and upgraded turbo coolant and oil lines.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting through our vetted network ensures your OM629 engine is installed by specialists equipped for heavy V8 diesel extraction, backed by a nationwide warranty.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: Because the OM629 is typically found in W211, W221, W164, and X164 vehicles valued between £5,000 and £18,000 for standard examples, a full replacement can represent a significant portion of the host's worth. If the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing .

items.question: How much does a Mercedes OM629 engine replacement cost?
items.answer: A reconditioned Mercedes OM629 engine typically costs between £3,500 and £5,500 for supply only . Fitted costs generally range from £5,000 to £7,800 depending on the specialist, while used units can be found from £1,500 but carry a high financial risk due to the engine's complex failure profile. items.question: What is the most common failure on the OM629 engine?
items.answer: The most documented issues are turbocharger oil feed line coking, injector seal weeping ("Black Death"), and EGR/swirl flap carbon buildup. Coked oil lines can starve the twin turbos and cause catastrophic bearing failure, while injector seal failure is a cheaper but mandatory preventative maintenance item. Get quotes for a rebuilt OM629 with these issues resolved

items.question: Which Mercedes models use the OM629 engine?
items.answer: The OM629 was fitted to the W211 E-Class (E 420 CDI), the W221 S-Class (S 420 CDI), the W164 M-Class (ML 420 CDI), and the X164 GL-Class (GL 420 CDI), serving as Mercedes' premium V8 diesel for their heaviest chassis between 2005 and 2010. items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned OM629 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned OM629 is strongly recommended over a used unit. A proper rebuild will proactively address the fatal flaws by installing upgraded turbo oil feed lines, verifying piezo injector spray patterns, and replacing all injector seals, whereas a used engine with unknown history often leads to an immediate £3,000+ teardown bill if the turbos fail shortly after installation. items.question: How do I know if my car has the OM629 and not the OM628 or OM642?
items.answer: The OM629 is a 4.0L V8 diesel with piezo-electric injectors, distinct from the solenoid-injected OM628 or the 3.0L V6 OM642. The engine code is stamped on the left-hand side of the cylinder block near the bellhousing and is also listed on your V5C logbook.
